summary: Describes a public extension key for iSCSI that lets nodes tell each other details about their architecture during login. The receiving side can use that information to improve supportability and troubleshooting. It builds on the extension-key mechanism in RFC 3720 and was later replaced by RFC 7143.

plainLanguage.summary: When two machines meet, they can quickly say what kind of machine they are. This helps the people fixing problems later know what they are dealing with.

subtitle: How iSCSI nodes tell each other their architecture during login.

tldr.problem: When two iSCSI systems connect, the receiving side has no standard way to learn details about the sender's software, firmware, hardware, or operating system, making troubleshooting and support difficult.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4850 defines a declarative public extension key called X#NodeArchitecture that iSCSI nodes can send during login to advertise their architecture details—vendor software versions, firmware versions, OS, hardware type, and similar information.
tldr.outcome: Support teams gain visibility into the systems they are troubleshooting, and vendors can improve compatibility by understanding which versions interact with which systems. RFC 7143 later updated the iSCSI protocol and superseded this RFC.

today: RFC 4850 defined the X#NodeArchitecture extension key and updated RFC 3720 to allow standards track and experimental RFCs to define extension items. This RFC was superseded by RFC 7143, which consolidated and updated the iSCSI protocol specification. Implementations should consult RFC 7143 for current requirements.

sections.title: iSCSI Extension Keys and Supportability
sections.content:
The iSCSI protocol, defined in RFC 3720, is a protocol for sending block storage commands over IP networks. During login, two iSCSI nodes negotiate operational parameters using a mechanism that supports extension keys. These keys allow nodes to exchange information beyond what the core protocol requires.

RFC 4850 defines one specific extension key called X#NodeArchitecture whose purpose is to improve supportability and troubleshooting. When support teams investigate problems between iSCSI systems, understanding each system's architecture helps them diagnose compatibility issues and advise on configurations.
sections.plainLanguage: iSCSI is a way to send disk commands over the network. During the handshake, you can exchange extra notes. One note can say what kind of system you are.

sections.title: The X#NodeArchitecture Key
sections.content:
The X#NodeArchitecture key carries a comma-separated list of text values describing the sending node's architecture. Examples include the operating system name and version, vendor software and version numbers, firmware version, hardware architecture (like CPU type), or any other component details the vendor deems relevant.

The key is sent during the operational parameter negotiation phase of login, after security negotiation is complete, and only on the leading connection of a session. A receiving node that does not recognize this key responds with X#NodeArchitecture=NotUnderstood, allowing graceful interoperability with older nodes that follow RFC 3720 strictly. The maximum length of the key's value is 255 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: During login, a node can send a text message like "Linux 5.10, iSCSI-Initiator-2.1, Intel CPU". The other side reads it to understand what kind of system is connecting. Old systems that don't understand this just ignore it.

sections.title: Implementation and Functional Requirements
sections.content:
A node implementing X#NodeArchitecture must choose one of three modes: transmit the key, log received keys, or both. The key is declarative, meaning the node itself sets the values; there is no mechanism for an external administrator to insert arbitrary text into the key, reducing the risk of false advertising.

Critically, the RFC emphasizes that functional behavior must not depend on this key. A node that sends detailed architecture information must work equally well with nodes that receive and ignore it. The key is purely informational and must never be used to exclude or discriminate between nodes during interoperability checks or for any protocol decision.
sections.plainLanguage: You choose whether to send your info or just listen. Either way, the system works the same. You never decide to reject someone based on their architecture info.

sections.title: Security Tradeoffs and Disclosure
sections.content:
Because the key reveals implementation details, a concern exists in security-sensitive environments. A node advertising a software version known to contain a vulnerability could attract targeted attacks. Countermeasures include: sending less detailed information (omitting version numbers), disabling the key entirely, or using IPsec to encrypt the iSCSI session. The RFC requires that all implementations provide an administrative mechanism to disable key transmission and recommends the ability to configure verbosity levels.

Different systems may have different risk profiles. A high-value iSCSI target with tight security might disable transmission and not log received values. Initiators in a blade farm running general-purpose operating systems might transmit the key for support purposes but discard received values. The appropriate choice depends on the organization's security posture and the role of the system.
sections.plainLanguage: If you announce your version, attackers might target that version. You can turn it off, or send less detail. High-security systems might be silent; others might broadcast for support. Pick what fits your situation.
